back: One deployable unit containing all the application's code. It can still run as many copies behind a load balancer.
A single deployable whose modules each own their code and tables and only call each other through defined interfaces, often enforced by build checks.

front: Name three strengths of a monolith.
back: Fast, reliable in-process calls; easy single-database transactions; one thing to deploy, monitor and debug.
A separately deployable service that owns one business capability and its own data, talking to others over the network.

front: What are the main benefits of microservices?
back: Independent deploys, clear team ownership, independent scaling, fault isolation (if callers handle failure) and per-service technology choice.

front: In-process call vs same-datacentre service call: rough latency?
back: About 100 ns in process vs roughly 0.5–few ms across the network once serialisation and the other service's work are included.
Some parts of a distributed operation succeed while others fail or are unknown, e.g. a call times out after the server already did the work.

front: What replaces a database transaction across services?
back: Patterns like sagas: a sequence of local transactions with compensating actions, plus acceptance of temporary inconsistency.
Services that must be deployed together or share a database: microservice costs without microservice independence.
Organisations design systems that mirror their own communication structure.

front: What is the inverse Conway manoeuvre?
back: Shaping teams around the business capabilities you want first, so the service boundaries that follow team boundaries are the right ones.

front: Split services by technical layer or by business capability?
back: Business capability. Layer splits make nearly every feature change several services and teams.
Start with a monolith until you understand the domain, because moving a service boundary is far more expensive than moving a module boundary.

front: Name two good reasons to split one module into a service.
back: A very different scaling profile (CPU/GPU/bursty), or a need for a separate release cadence or security boundary, once boundaries are stable.

front: What is the strangler fig pattern?
back: Put a router in front of the old system and move one capability at a time to new services until the old code can be deleted.
